meta.description: Yes, it's Napoleon Hill — Think and Grow Rich (1937), chapter 7. His actual wording: “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No man is ever whipped until he quits in his own mind'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Napoleon Hill, from Think and Grow Rich (1937), ch. 7 — verified in two scans. The popular version quietly drops his commas and capitals.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Hill wrote it in Think and Grow Rich (first published 1937), chapter 7, “Organized Planning: The Crystallization of Desire into Action.” The book’s own wording carries commas and a capitalised verb — “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind” — and the sentence appears exactly once, confirmed against two independent full-text scans.

source.excerpt: No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind. This fact will be repeated many times, because it is so easy to “take the count” at the first sign of defeat.
trail: The sentence is in the full text of Think and Grow Rich ↗, in chapter 7, “Organized Planning” — reading “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind.”

A second, independent scan ↗ with different pagination carries the identical sentence in the same chapter, immediately after the same Samuel Insull passage — so this is the book’s text, not one transcriber’s slip.

Hill was working the image well before 1937: The Law of Success (1928) ↗ says of the Dempsey–Tunney fight that “Dempsey was whipped, in his own mind, before he entered the ring,” and prints “A WINNER NEVER QUITS, AND A QUITTER NEVER WINS.” The 1937 sentence itself does not appear there.

The specialists have not weighed in: a Quote Investigator site search ↗ returns nothing, and the line is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced Napoleon Hill quotations ↗ — so this page rests on the book itself.
source.excerptNote: Hill sets this down immediately after a passage on Samuel Insull, whose fortune collapsed when the Depression forced him to change plans that had been sound. The sentence appears exactly once in the book; a few paragraphs later Hill adds the separate slogan “A QUITTER NEVER WINS—AND— A WINNER NEVER QUITS.”

source.rightsNote: Think and Grow Rich was first published in 1937, well after the 1931 line for automatic US public domain, and the Napoleon Hill Foundation ↗ publishes authorised editions and owns the registered trademark Think and Grow Rich®, directing reprint and republication requests to it. Some free-ebook reprinters assert the original 1937 text has lapsed into the public domain for want of a renewal — Stanford’s renewal index ↗ lists only three records for the title, all covering 1960 publications — but we do not resolve that and treat the book conservatively as in–copyright.

author.name: Napoleon Hill
author.heading: The man who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1883–1970 · American self-help author; wrote Think and Grow Rich (1937)
author.bio: Napoleon Hill wrote the books that set the template for the modern success genre: The Law of Success (1928), then Think and Grow Rich (1937), still the book he is known for. He said the philosophy grew out of work commissioned by Andrew Carnegie, but Wikipedia’s article — which opens by describing Hill as a self-help author and con man — notes that the Carnegie collaboration has remained unsupported by any evidence, and that historians doubt his claims to have been an attorney or to have advised Presidents Wilson and Roosevelt. The sentences in his books are genuinely his; a good deal of what he claimed about his own life is not.

misattribution.heading: Right author, edited sentence
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare cases where a famous motivational line survives the fact-check: Napoleon Hill really did write it, and it is easy to find in his best-known book. What has not survived is his punctuation — and, in circulation, the source almost never travels with the words.

items.why: The sentence that circulates — “No man is ever whipped until he quits in his own mind” — has been tidied. The book itself ↗ reads “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind,” with two commas, a capitalised verb and a dash that Hill used for emphasis.

A further-drifted rendering circulates in print. A 2010s leadership book quotes it as “A man is never whipped until he quits in his own mind,” credited to Hill with no source given — visible alongside the correct readings in Goodreads’ quote search ↗.

items.who: “A quitter never wins and a winner never quits”
items.why: Hill prints this second slogan a few paragraphs later in the same chapter, and had already used it in The Law of Success (1928) ↗. The two are frequently blended or swapped for each other, but they are separate sentences.

The line spreads as a bare attribution to Hill’s name. Quote Investigator has never examined it — a site search returns nothing ↗ — and it does not appear among the sourced quotations on Wikiquote’s Napoleon Hill page ↗, so most people repeating it have no citation to hand.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are both Hill’s: Think and Grow Rich, chapter 7 ↗, first published 1937 — just with two commas and a shout that the internet has quietly edited out.

context.heading: Why Hill wrote it there
lead: The line is not a standalone slogan in the book. It lands in the middle of chapter 7, Hill’s chapter on building — and rebuilding — practical plans, immediately after a passage about Samuel Insull, the utilities magnate whose fortune collapsed when the Depression forced him to change plans that had been sound. Hill’s argument in that chapter is narrow and practical: a failure means your plan was wrong, so build another one, and again, until one works. The sentence is the emotional hinge of that argument, not a general life motto.

Hill knew he was writing a refrain. He follows it with a note that the fact “will be repeated many times, because it is so easy to ‘take the count’ at the first sign of defeat” — boxing language, and a hint at where the image came from. Nine years earlier, in The Law of Success (1928), he had already written that Jack Dempsey “was whipped, in his own mind, before he entered the ring” against Gene Tunney. The 1937 sentence is Hill compressing an idea he had been working with for a decade into twelve words.
context.detailsSummary: Is the book itself in the public domain?
detailsBody: You will see Think and Grow Rich offered as a free public-domain ebook, and some of those editions state on their own legal page that the 1937 text is now public domain. That claim rests on the renewal rule for US works published between 1929 and 1963: copyright had to be renewed in its 28th year or it lapsed. Stanford’s index of copyright renewals returns only three records for the title, and all three cover 1960 publications — the revised edition and an Earl Nightingale condensation — renewed in September 1988 by David H. Hill.

That absence is not a legal ruling, and the Napoleon Hill Foundation continues to publish authorised editions and owns the registered trademark Think and Grow Rich®. Quotle.info does not resolve the question: because the work was first published well after 1931 and an active rights holder asserts rights over it, we classify it conservatively as in–copyright.
context.pull: Hill flagged it himself: “This fact will be repeated many times.” It has been — just rarely with his commas.

sourcesVerified.claim: Think and Grow Rich, chapter 7 (“Organized Planning: The Crystallization of Desire into Action”), contains the sentence “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind,” followed by “This fact will be repeated many times…”, and a few paragraphs later “A QUITTER NEVER WINS—AND— A WINNER NEVER QUITS.”
An independent second scan of Think and Grow Rich, with different pagination, carries the identical sentence in chapter 7, immediately following the Samuel Insull passage.

The Law of Success (1928) contains “Dempsey was whipped, in his own mind, before he entered the ring” and “A WINNER NEVER QUITS, AND A QUITTER NEVER WINS”, but not the sentence “No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS— in his own mind.”

Wikipedia gives Napoleon Hill's dates as October 26, 1883 – November 8, 1970, describes him in the lead as “an American self-help author and con man” best known for Think and Grow Rich (1937), states that his collaboration with Andrew Carnegie “has remained unsupported by any evidence,” and notes the Napoleon Hill Foundation was established in 1963.
Wikipedia gives 1937 as the first publication year of Think and Grow Rich.

Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill page carries sourced quotations from The Law of Success and Think and Grow Rich with page numbers, but contains no quotation with the words “whipped” or “quits in his own mind”, and has no Misattributed or Disputed section.
A Quote Investigator site search for “quits in his own mind” returns no results — QI has not investigated this quotation.

The Napoleon Hill Foundation owns registered trademarks including Think and Grow Rich®, states it routinely challenges unauthorised uses, and directs reprint or republication requests to rights@naphill.org.

Goodreads' quote search shows the correct book wording (“No man is ever whipped, until he QUITS - in his own mind”, Think and Grow Rich) alongside a drifted rendering, “A man is never whipped until he quits in his own mind,” credited to Napoleon Hill inside a later leadership book by Christy Rutherford.

Stanford's Copyright Renewal Database returns exactly three renewal records titled “Think and grow rich”, all for 1960 publication dates (12 Jul 1960, 26 May 1960, 29 Jul 1960), all renewed 19 Sep 1988 by claimant David H. Hill; no renewal record for the 1937 first edition appears.
